```{webr-r}
#| autorun: true

library(data.table)
library(ggplot2)
library(patchwork)
library(broom)
library(pROC)

theme_set(
  theme_bw(base_size = 14) +
  theme(
    panel.grid = element_blank(),
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 12),
    axis.title = element_text(size = 12)
  )

```

## Today

We'll shift from using models to **describe relationships** to using them to **predict outcomes** for individuals.

- How can we evaluate whether a model will predict well for new people?
- What makes a predicted probability useful?
- How can we use predicted probabilities to classify individuals?
- What tradeoffs arise when we change the threshold used for classification?
- Does a more flexible model necessarily make better predictions?

These questions shift our focus from **explaining the data we have observed** to **how well a model performs on new data**.

## From modeling a relationship to making a prediction

In Lecture 6, we considered the relationship between **age and hypertension**.

We asked:

> ***How does the probability of hypertension change with age?***

Logistic regression was used to model that relationship:

$$\large
\operatorname{logit}\left[P(Y=1\mid\text{age})\right]
=
\beta_0+\beta_1(\text{age})$$

Our goal was primarily to **describe and estimate a relationship**.

For example, we could use the model to estimate how the odds or probability of hypertension differ with age.


### A different question

Now suppose we conduct a **longitudinal study**. At baseline, we record each person's age. We then follow everyone for **5 years** and determine whether they develop hypertension.

For each person, define

$$\large
Y =
\begin{cases}
1 & \text{if hypertension develops within 5 years} \\
0 & \text{otherwise}
\end{cases}$$

We could still fit a logistic regression model:

$$\large
\operatorname{logit}\left[P(Y=1\mid\text{age})\right]
=
\beta_0+\beta_1(\text{age})$$

But now suppose our question is:

> ***Can we use what we know about a person today to predict whether they will develop hypertension during the next 5 years?***

The model may look the same, but our **goal has changed**.

Rather than focusing primarily on the *relationship* between age and hypertension, we want to know how well information available **today** can *predict* an outcome that will occur in the **future**.

### Different questions and different goals

The same variables — and sometimes even the same statistical model — can be used to address **different scientific questions**.

<div style="margin-top: 3rem;"></div>

| **Objective** | **Fundamental question** | **What does it help us do?** |
|---|---|---|
| **Description / association** | How are variables related in a population? | Understand populations, identify patterns and disparities, generate hypotheses |
| **Prediction** | What is likely to happen to a new individual? | Prognosis, risk stratification, screening, resource allocation |
| **Causal inference / intervention** | What would happen if we changed something? | Choose treatments, policies, programs, or interventions |

<div style="margin-top: 3rem;"></div>

## From data to a model to a prediction

Let's simulate data from a longitudinal study. For each person, we observe their **age at baseline** and whether they develop **hypertension during the next 5 years**.

#### Generating the data

```{webr-r}
set.seed(12345)

DGP <- function(n, beta_age = 0.075) {
  
  d <- data.table(
    age = runif(n, 20, 80)
  )

  d[, p := plogis(-1.75 + beta_age * (age - 50))]
  d[, hypertension_5yr := rbinom(.N, size = 1, prob = p)]

  return(d)
}

dd <- DGP(500)

dd[, .(age, hypertension_5yr)]
```

#### Fitting a model and generating predictions

```{webr-r}
fit <- glm(
  hypertension_5yr ~ age,
  data = dd,
  family = binomial
)

dd[, predicted_risk := predict(fit, type = "response")]

dd[, .(age, hypertension_5yr, predicted_risk)]
```

#### Visualizing data

```{webr-r}
#| classes: webr-plot

ggplot(
  data = dd, 
  aes(x = age, y = predicted_risk)
) +
  geom_point(
    aes(
      x = age, 
      y = hypertension_5yr
    ), 
    size = 0.7
  ) +
  geom_line()
```

The model gives us an estimated probability for each person. For example, a predicted risk of 0.30 means that the model estimates a **30% probability of developing hypertension within 5 years** for a person of that age.

Notice that the prediction is a **probability**, even though the outcome itself is binary.

> ***But how do we know whether these predicted probabilities are any good?***



## How well does our model predict?

We have fit a model using data from 500 people.

We could evaluate its predictions by comparing them with the outcomes we actually observed for those same 500 people.

But remember our goal:

> **We want to predict outcomes for new people.**

The 500 people used to fit the model are **not new people** — the model has already seen their data.

So there are two different questions:

> **How well does the model predict outcomes for the people used to fit it?**
>
> **How well will the model predict outcomes for new people?**

For prediction, it is the **second question** that matters.


### Learning from one sample

Suppose our 500 people are a sample from a much larger population.

- We use their baseline information and subsequent outcomes to **train** our prediction model.

- The fitted model has learned patterns from this particular sample.

- Some of those patterns reflect real relationships in the population.

- But some may simply reflect **random variation in this particular sample**.

> **Patterns that reflect random variation in the training data may not help us predict outcomes in new people.**


### Learning signal — or learning noise?

Because we are simulating the data, we know that **age is the only predictor of future hypertension**.

Now suppose we generate 20 other baseline characteristics so that they have **no relationship whatsoever** with future hypertension.

```{webr-r}
set.seed(2718)

noise_vars <- paste0("x", 1:20)

dd[, (noise_vars) := lapply(
  1:20,
  function(j) rnorm(.N)
)]

dd[, .(x1, x9, x13, x20)]
```

Imagine that we don't know which variables are actually useful predictors.

We could fit the simple model using only age:

```{webr-r}
fit_simple <- glm(
  hypertension_5yr ~ age,
  data = dd,
  family = binomial
)
```

Or we could fit the extended, more complicated model using age and all 20 additional variables:

```{webr-r}
fit_extended <- glm(
  hypertension_5yr ~ .,
  data = dd[, 
    c("hypertension_5yr", "age", noise_vars), 
    with = FALSE
  ],
  family = binomial
)
```

We know something the analyst would not know:

> ***None of the 20 additional variables contains any real information about future hypertension.***

But in a sample of 500 people, some of them will be associated with hypertension **just by chance**.


### Which model predicts the observed data better?

For each person, we can compare the predicted probability with what actually happened. If someone develops hypertension, their outcome is 1. If they do not, their outcome is 0.

One simple measure of prediction error is

$$\large
\text{Prediction error}
=
\frac{1}{n}
\sum_{i=1}^{n}
(Y_i-\hat p_i)^2$$

Smaller values indicate predictions that are closer to the observed outcomes.

```{webr-r}
dd[, 
  pred_simple := predict(fit_simple, type = "response")]

dd[,
  pred_extended := predict(fit_extended, type = "response")]

dd[, .(
  simple = mean((hypertension_5yr - pred_simple)^2),
  extended = mean((hypertension_5yr - pred_extended)^2)
)]
```

> **The extended model has a smaller prediction error.**

But remember: **we evaluated the models using the same data that were used to fit them.**


### What happens with new people?

Now let's generate 500 **new people from exactly the same population**.

```{webr-r}
set.seed(8172)

dd_new <- DGP(500)

dd_new[, (noise_vars) := lapply(
  1:20,
  function(j) rnorm(.N)
)]
```

These people were not used to estimate either model.

Let's use the two fitted models to predict their outcomes:

```{webr-r}
dd_new[, pred_simple := predict(
  fit_simple,
  newdata = dd_new,
  type = "response"
)]

dd_new[, pred_extended := predict(
  fit_extended,
  newdata = dd_new,
  type = "response"
)]

dd_new[, .(
  simple = mean((hypertension_5yr - pred_simple)^2),
  extended = mean((hypertension_5yr - pred_extended)^2)
)]
```


> In the original data, the extended model had **lower prediction error** than the simple model.
>
> When we applied both models to new people, the extended model had **higher prediction error**.

The extended model learned some patterns that were specific to the original sample. Those patterns helped it predict the data it had already seen, but they did not help it predict outcomes for new people. This is **overfitting**.

> **A model can fit the observed data well because it has learned both real signal and random noise.**


## Training and test data


In our simulation, we could simply generate another sample of 500 people to see how well the models performed on new data. *In a real study, we usually cannot do that.*

Instead, one approach is to divide the data we have into two parts:

- **Training data:** used to fit the model
- **Test data:** set aside and used to evaluate how well the fitted model predicts outcomes for observations it has not seen

For example, we might randomly use 80% of our observations for training and reserve 20% for testing.

```{webr-r}
set.seed(2026)

train_id <- sample(
  1:nrow(dd),
  size = 0.80 * nrow(dd)
)

train_data <- dd[train_id]
test_data <- dd[-train_id]
```

```{webr-r}
nrow(train_data)
nrow(test_data)
```

- We would fit our prediction model using the 400 people in the training data.
- We would then use that fitted model to generate predictions for the 100 people in the test data and evaluate those predictions.
- The crucial point is that the test data play the role that our 500 newly generated people played in the simulation:

**They give us observations that were not used to fit the model.**

This allows us to estimate how well the model generalizes to new observations.


### What if the results depend on how we split the data?

A single training/test split has its own randomness. Different observations could have ended up in the training and test sets.

Suppose we are deciding between two prediction models and we want to know which one will predict better for **new people**.

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{Model 1: }& \text{age}\\
\text{Model 2: }& \text{age + BMI + physical activity}
\end{aligned}
$$

**Cross-validation** lets us compare them without relying on a single arbitrary split.

We divide the training data into several parts, or **folds**. For each model:

- fit the model using all but one fold
- evaluate its predictions on the fold that was left out
- repeat until every fold has been left out once
- **average the predictive performance across the folds**

We can then compare the average performance of Model 1 and Model 2 and **choose the model specification**.

> **Cross-validation helps us choose the model specification — we are not averaging the parameter estimates from the different fits.**

Once we have selected a model, we fit it again using **all of the training data**.

Finally, we use the **untouched test data** to evaluate how well this one final model predicts new observations.

> **We do not use the test data to choose between models.**

## Are the predicted probabilities accurate?

In Lecture 6, we evaluated logistic regression by comparing **predicted probabilities** with what we actually observed.

For example, if a model predicts risks around 30%, we would hope that roughly 30% of comparable people actually have the outcome.

For prediction, we can ask the same question — but now we want to know whether this relationship holds in **new data**.

> ***If the model predicts a 30% risk of developing hypertension, do about 30% of similar people actually develop hypertension?***

This is called **calibration**.


#### One important point

Suppose a person has a predicted risk of 70% and does **not** develop hypertension.

That does not mean the prediction was wrong.

A probability describes what we would expect to happen across many similar people, not what must happen to one individual.

### Let's evaluate calibration in the new sample of 500 people . . .

We will start by **ordering the 500 people according to their predicted risk**.

Then we divide them into five equally sized groups:

- the 100 people with the **lowest predicted risks**
- the next 100 people
- the next 100 people
- the next 100 people
- the 100 people with the **highest predicted risks**

> **These groups are determined by predicted risk — they are not formed randomly.**

Within each group, we compare:

- the **average predicted risk**
- the **proportion who actually developed hypertension**

```{webr-r}
dd_new[, risk_group := cut(
  pred_simple,
  breaks = quantile(
    pred_simple,
    probs = seq(0, 1, by = 0.2)
  ),
  include.lowest = TRUE,
  labels = c(
    "Lowest risk",
    "Low risk",
    "Middle risk",
    "High risk",
    "Highest risk"
  )
)]

calibration <- dd_new[,
  .(predicted = mean(pred_simple),
    observed = mean(hypertension_5yr)
  ),
  keyby = risk_group
]

calibration
```

```{webr-r}
#| classes: webr-plot

ggplot(
  calibration, 
  aes(x = predicted, y = observed)
) +
  geom_abline(
    intercept = 0, 
    slope = 1, 
    linetype = 2
  ) +
  geom_point(
    size = 3,
    aes(color = risk_group)
  ) +
  coord_equal(
    xlim = c(0, 0.6), 
    ylim = c(0, 0.6)
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "Average predicted risk",
    y = "Observed proportion with hypertension"
  ) +
  theme(legend.title = element_blank()) +
  guides(color = guide_legend(reverse = TRUE))
```

If the predicted and observed probabilities agreed perfectly, the points would fall along the diagonal line.

We do not expect perfect agreement because the observed proportions are themselves subject to **sampling variability**.

> **Calibration asks whether predicted probabilities correspond to what actually happens in new data.**

If a model is poorly calibrated in new data, its predicted probabilities may not be reliable in that population.

> **A prediction model should be evaluated in the population where we intend to use it.**



## From predicted probabilities to decisions


So far, our model has produced **predicted probabilities**. But sometimes we want to use those probabilities **to make a decision**.

Suppose we want to identify people at sufficiently high risk of developing hypertension that they should receive **additional monitoring**.

> ***How high does someone's predicted risk need to be before we classify them as "high risk"?***

We need to choose a **classification threshold**.

Suppose we start with a threshold of 0.30:

$$\large
\text{Classified high risk}
=
\begin{cases}
1 & \text{if predicted risk} \geq 0.30\\
0 & \text{if predicted risk} < 0.30
\end{cases}$$

```{webr-r}
dd_new[, 
  classified_high_risk := as.integer(pred_simple >= 0.30)]

dd_new[1:10, 
  .(predicted_risk = pred_simple, 
    hypertension_5yr, 
    classified_high_risk
  )
]

# also look at 0.20, 0.40
```

Now every person has two pieces of information:

- their classification based on the predicted risk
- what actually happened


### What can happen when we use this decision rule?

For each person, we compare their **classification** with what eventually happens.

<div style="margin-top: 5em;"></div>

|                          | Hypertension   | No hypertension |
|--------------------------|----------------|-----------------|
| **Classified high risk** | True positive  | False positive  |
| **Classified low risk**  | False negative | True negative   |

<div style="margin-top: 5rem;"></div>

These terms describe the performance of the **classification rule** relative to the eventual outcome.

They do not mean that someone's predicted probability was "right" or "wrong."


### Generating the classification/misclassification table

```{webr-r}
class_tab <- table(
  Classified = factor(
    dd_new$classified_high_risk,
    levels = c(1, 0),
    labels = c("High risk", "Low risk")
  ),
  Observed = factor(
    dd_new$hypertension_5yr,
    levels = c(1, 0),
    labels = c("Hypertension", "No hypertension")
  )
)

class_tab
```

<div style="margin-top: 3em;"></div>
<div style="font-size: 0.75em;">

|                          | Hypertension   | No hypertension |
|--------------------------|----------------|-----------------|
| **Classified high risk** | True positive  | False positive  |
| **Classified low risk**  | False negative | True negative   |

</div>
<div style="margin-top: 3em;"></div>


### How many people who develop hypertension do we identify?

Suppose we focus first on the people **who actually developed hypertension**.

Among these people, what proportion were classified as high risk?

$$\large
\text{Sensitivity}
=
\frac{\text{True positives}}
{\text{True positives}+\text{False negatives}}$$

```{webr-r}
class_tab["High risk", "Hypertension"] /
  sum(class_tab[, "Hypertension"])
```

> This is the **sensitivity** of the classification rule: the proportion of people who **developed hypertension** who had been classified as **high risk**.

<div style="margin-top: 3em;"></div>
<div style="font-size: 0.75em;">

|                          | Hypertension   | No hypertension |
|--------------------------|----------------|-----------------|
| **Classified high risk** | <span style="background-color: #ffff99; padding: 3px 6px;">**True positive**</span>  | False positive |
| **Classified low risk**  | <span style="background-color: #ffff99; padding: 3px 6px;">**False negative**</span>  | True negative |

</div>
<div style="margin-top: 3em;"></div>


### How many people who do not develop hypertension are classified as low risk?

Now consider the people who did **not** develop hypertension.

Among these people, what proportion were classified as low risk?

$$\large
\text{Specificity}
=
\frac{\text{True negatives}}
{\text{True negatives}+\text{False positives}}$$

```{webr-r}
class_tab["Low risk", "No hypertension"] /
  sum(class_tab[, "No hypertension"])
```

> This is the **specificity** of the classification rule: the proportion of people who did **not develop hypertension** who had been classified as **low risk**.

<div style="margin-top: 3em;"></div>
<div style="font-size: 0.75em;">

|                          | Hypertension   | No hypertension |
|--------------------------|----------------|-----------------|
| **Classified high risk** | True positive  | <span style="background-color: #ffff99; padding: 3px 6px;">**False positive**</span>  |
| **Classified low risk**  | False negative | <span style="background-color: #ffff99; padding: 3px 6px;">**True negative**</span> |

</div>
<div style="margin-top: 3em;"></div>

### What about the people incorrectly classified as high risk?

Specificity tells us the proportion of people **without hypertension** who are correctly classified as low risk.

We can ask the complementary question:

> ***Among people who do not develop hypertension, what proportion are incorrectly classified as high risk?***

This is the **false positive rate**:

$$\large
\text{False positive rate}
=
\frac{\text{False positives}}
{\text{True negatives}+\text{False positives}}
$$

Because everyone without hypertension is classified as either low risk or high risk:

$$\large
\text{False positive rate} = 1 - \text{Specificity}
$$

```{webr-r}
class_tab["High risk", "No hypertension"] /
  sum(class_tab[, "No hypertension"])
```

> The **false positive rate** is the proportion of people who did **not develop hypertension** who had been classified as **high risk**.

<div style="margin-top: 3em;"></div>
<div style="font-size: 0.75em;">

|                          | Hypertension   | No hypertension |
|--------------------------|----------------|-----------------|
| **Classified high risk** | True positive  | <span style="background-color: #ffff99; padding: 3px 6px;">**False positive**</span> |
| **Classified low risk**  | False negative | <span style="background-color: #ffff99; padding: 3px 6px;">**True negative**</span> |

</div>

### What if we start with the people classified as high risk?

Sensitivity asks:

> Among people who **develop hypertension**, how many were classified as high risk?

We can also ask the question in the other direction:

> Among people **classified as high risk**, how many actually develop hypertension?

This is the **positive predictive value (PPV)**:

$$\large
\text{PPV}
=
\frac{\text{True positives}}
{\text{True positives}+\text{False positives}}
$$

```{webr-r}
class_tab["High risk", "Hypertension"] /
  sum(class_tab["High risk",])
```


<div style="margin-top: 3em;"></div>
<div style="font-size: 0.75em;">

|                          | Hypertension   | No hypertension |
|--------------------------|----------------|-----------------|
| **Classified high risk** | <span style="background-color: #ffff99; padding: 3px 6px;">**True positive**</span>  | <span style="background-color: #ffff99; padding: 3px 6px;">**False positive**</span> |
| **Classified low risk**  | False negative | True negative |

</div>

### What happens if we change the threshold?

So far, we have used a classification threshold of 0.30, which was an arbitrary choice.

If we **lower the threshold**, more people will be classified as high risk.

This means:

- we will identify more of the people who develop hypertension  
  $\rightarrow$ **sensitivity increases**
- we will also classify more people who do not develop hypertension as high risk  
  $\rightarrow$ **false positive rate increases**

If we **raise the threshold**, the opposite happens.

> **Choosing a classification threshold involves a tradeoff between identifying people who will develop the outcome and incorrectly classifying people who will not.**

Which tradeoff is appropriate depends in part on the **consequences of the classification**.

For example, if being classified as high risk simply leads to additional blood pressure monitoring, false positives may have relatively little cost.

In another setting, false positives might have substantial costs or harms.


## From one threshold to many thresholds

We saw that changing the classification threshold changes who is classified as
high risk.

Let's look at three possible thresholds and see exactly what happens. For each threshold, focus on two quantities:

- **Sensitivity:** among people who develop hypertension, what proportion did we classify as high risk?
- **False positive rate:** among people who do **not** develop hypertension, what proportion did we nevertheless classify as high risk?


```{webr-r}
threshold_summary <- function(threshold) {

  classified <- as.integer(dd_new$pred_simple >= threshold)

  data.table(
    threshold = threshold,
    sensitivity = mean(
      classified[dd_new$hypertension_5yr == 1]
    ),
    false_positive_rate = mean(
      classified[dd_new$hypertension_5yr == 0]
    )
  )
}

threshold_results <- rbindlist(
  lapply(c(0.50, 0.30, 0.10), threshold_summary)
)

threshold_results
```

## Representing a threshold with a point

We can represent each threshold with a point:

- **False positive rate** on the horizontal axis
- **Sensitivity** on the vertical axis

Let's start with the threshold of 0.30.

```{webr-r}
#| classes: webr-plot

ggplot(
  threshold_results[threshold == 0.30],
  aes(x = false_positive_rate, y = sensitivity)
) +
  geom_point(size = 5) +
  coord_equal(
    xlim = c(0, 1),
    ylim = c(0, 1),
    expand = FALSE
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "False positive rate",
    y = "Sensitivity"
  )
```

### Now change the threshold

Let's add the thresholds of 0.50 and 0.10.

```{webr-r}
#| classes: webr-plot

ggplot(
  threshold_results,
  aes(x = false_positive_rate, y = sensitivity)
) +
  geom_point(size = 5) +
  geom_text(
    aes(label = threshold),
    nudge_y = 0.05
  ) +
  coord_equal(
    xlim = c(0, 1),
    ylim = c(0, 1),
    expand = FALSE
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "False positive rate",
    y = "Sensitivity"
  )
```

Notice what happens as we **lower** the threshold:

> **The points move up and to the right.**

- **Up:** sensitivity increases.
- **Right:** the false positive rate increases.

This is the tradeoff created by changing the classification threshold.

#### Where would we like to be?

Before adding any more thresholds, think about the two axes.

For a useful classifier, we would like:

- **high sensitivity** → move **up**
- **low false positive rate** → move **left**

So where would the ideal point be?

> ***The upper-left corner.***

A point near the upper-left would mean that we identify most people who
develop hypertension while falsely classifying relatively few people who do
not.

---

## What if we consider every possible threshold?

There is nothing special about 0.50, 0.30, or 0.10.

We could repeat exactly the same calculation for every possible classification
threshold. Each threshold gives us another $(\text{false positive rate},\ \text{sensitivity})$ combination. If we plot all of those points and connect them, we get a curve.

```{webr-r}
#| classes: webr-plot

thresholds <- c(
  Inf,
  sort(unique(dd_new$pred_simple), decreasing = TRUE),
  -Inf
)

roc <- rbindlist(lapply(thresholds, function(threshold) {

  classified <- as.integer(dd_new$pred_simple >= threshold)

  data.table(
    threshold = threshold,
    sensitivity = mean(
      classified[dd_new$hypertension_5yr == 1]
    ),
    false_positive_rate = mean(
      classified[dd_new$hypertension_5yr == 0]
    )
  )
}))

roc_plot <- ggplot(
  roc,
  aes(x = false_positive_rate, y = sensitivity)
) +
  geom_step() +
  coord_equal(
    xlim = c(0, 1),
    ylim = c(0, 1),
    expand = FALSE
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "False positive rate",
    y = "Sensitivity"
  )

roc_plot
```

This is called a **receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve**.

> **An ROC curve shows the combinations of sensitivity and false positive rate
> produced by different classification thresholds.**

### What would happen with no discrimination?

Suppose the predicted risks contained no information about who would develop
hypertension.

Then lowering the threshold would tend to classify people from both groups as
high risk at about the same rate.

For example, if 30% of people who do not develop hypertension were classified
as high risk, we would also expect about 30% of people who do develop
hypertension to be classified as high risk.

That means

$$\large
\text{Sensitivity} \approx \text{False positive rate}.
$$

Those points would lie along the diagonal.

```{webr-r}
#| classes: webr-plot

roc_plot +
  geom_abline(
    intercept = 0,
    slope = 1,
    linetype = 2
  )
```

The diagonal therefore represents **no discrimination**.

> **The farther the ROC curve moves above the diagonal and toward the
> upper-left corner, the better the model distinguishes people who develop
> hypertension from those who do not.**

## What determines discrimination?


Our ability to discriminate depends on how much information the predictors contain about the outcome.

Because we simulated our population, we can change the strength of the relationship between **age and future hypertension** and see what happens.

Recall that our population was generated using:

$$\large
\operatorname{logit}(p)
=
-1.75+\beta_{\text{age}}(\text{age}-50)$$

In our original population,

$$\large
\beta_{\text{age}}=0.075.$$

What happens if age is **less informative** — or **more informative** — about future hypertension?

```{webr-r}
#| classes: webr-plot

set.seed(12345)

beta_age <- 0.0  # try 0, 0.05, 0.15

dd <- DGP(500, beta_age)

fit <- glm(
  hypertension_5yr ~ age, 
  data = dd, 
  family = binomial
)

set.seed(82761)

dd_test <- DGP(500, beta_age)

dd_test[, 
  predicted_risk := 
    predict(fit, newdata = dd_test, type = "response")
]

thresholds <- c(
  Inf,
  sort(
    unique(dd_test$predicted_risk), 
    decreasing = TRUE
  ),
  -Inf
)

roc_test <- rbindlist(lapply(
  thresholds, function(threshold) {
    classified <- as.integer(
      dd_test$predicted_risk >= threshold
    )
    
    data.table(
      sensitivity = mean(
        classified[dd_test$hypertension_5yr == 1]
      ),
      false_positive_rate = mean(
        classified[dd_test$hypertension_5yr == 0]
      )
    )
  }
))

ggplot(
  roc_test, 
  aes(x = false_positive_rate, y = sensitivity)
) +
  geom_step() +
  geom_abline(
    intercept = 0, 
    slope = 1, 
    linetype = 2
  ) +
  coord_equal(
    xlim = c(0, 1),
    ylim = c(0, 1),
    expand = FALSE
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "False positive rate",
    y = "Sensitivity"
  )
```

As age becomes more informative about future hypertension:

- the ROC curve moves farther toward the **upper-left corner**
- discrimination improves

> **Discrimination reflects how well the model separates people who experience the outcome from those who do not.**

## Summarizing discrimination: the AUC

The ROC curve shows how well the model distinguishes the two groups across **all possible classification thresholds**.

We can summarize this discrimination with a single number: the **area under the ROC curve (AUC)**.

- **AUC = 0.50:** no discrimination
- **AUC = 1.00:** perfect discrimination
- **Higher AUC:** better discrimination

> **The AUC summarizes how well the model distinguishes people who develop the outcome from those who do not.**

Importantly, the AUC does **not** tell us which classification threshold to use.

Choosing a threshold depends on the consequences of **false positives and false negatives**.

### Seeing the area under the curve

```{webr-r}
#| classes: webr-plot

ggplot(
  roc, 
  aes(x = false_positive_rate, y = sensitivity)
) +
  geom_ribbon(
    aes(ymin = 0, ymax = sensitivity), 
    alpha = 0.25
  ) +
  geom_step() +
  geom_abline(
    intercept = 0, 
    slope = 1, 
    linetype = 2
  ) +
  coord_equal(
    xlim = c(0, 1), 
    ylim = c(0, 1), 
    expand = FALSE
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "False positive rate",
    y = "Sensitivity"
  )
```


### What is the AUC for our model?

We can calculate the AUC directly from the observed outcomes and predicted risks using the `roc()` and `auc()` functions in the `pROC` package:

```{webr-r}
roc_result <- pROC::roc(
  response = dd_new$hypertension_5yr,
  predictor = dd_new$pred_simple
)

pROC::auc(roc_result)
```

The AUC summarizes the model's ability to **discriminate** between people who develop hypertension and those who do not.

> **Higher AUC indicates better discrimination; an AUC of 0.50 indicates no discrimination.**


### Discrimination is not calibration

A model can be good at **ranking** people from lower to higher risk without getting the probabilities themselves right.

> **AUC describes discrimination — not calibration. A model can discriminate well while still producing poorly calibrated predicted probabilities.**



## Prediction problems come in many forms


We have focused on predicting whether someone will develop hypertension within 5 years — a **binary outcome**.

But prediction problems can involve many different kinds of outcomes.

For example, we might want to predict:

- a **continuous outcome**, such as blood pressure one year from now
- a **binary outcome**, such as whether someone will develop hypertension
- an outcome with **multiple categories**, such as low, moderate, or high cardiovascular risk

Different statistical models may be appropriate for different kinds of outcomes.

But regardless of the model, the fundamental prediction question is the same:

> ***How well does a model developed using one sample predict outcomes for new people?***


### There are many ways to build a prediction model

We used logistic regression because it was already familiar to us.

But many different statistical and machine-learning methods can be used to make predictions, including *decision trees*, *random forests*, and *neural networks*.

The distinction between traditional statistical modeling and machine learning is not always sharp.

Machine-learning methods often allow the data to determine more **flexible relationships** between predictors and outcomes, with a particular emphasis on **prediction** rather than interpretation of individual coefficients.

> **The ideas we have developed in this lecture apply regardless of how the prediction model is constructed.**


### Does greater flexibility lead to better predictions?

Flexible methods can capture complicated relationships in the data.

But greater flexibility also creates more opportunity to learn **random features of the training sample** that will not generalize to new people.

This is the problem of **overfitting** that we saw earlier.

That is why we evaluate prediction models using data that were **not used to develop them**.

> **A more flexible prediction method is not necessarily a better prediction method.**

## One last simulation: predictive performance varies too

We have evaluated our prediction model using one new sample of 500 people.

But that sample is just **one possible sample** from the population.

What would happen if we evaluated the **same fitted model** using many different samples?

```{webr-r}
set.seed(91723)

n_sims <- 500

auc_results <- replicate(n_sims, {

  # Generate a new test sample
  dd_test <- DGP(500)

  # Use the SAME fitted model to predict risk
  dd_test[, predicted_risk :=
    predict(
      fit_simple,
      newdata = dd_test,
      type = "response"
    )
  ]

  # Calculate AUC in this test sample
  as.numeric(
    auc(
      roc(
        dd_test$hypertension_5yr,
        dd_test$predicted_risk,
        quiet = TRUE
      )
    )
  )
})

auc_results[1:10]
```

We have not changed the model or the population. The only thing that changes is the **sample used to evaluate the model**.

Here is the **sampling distribution** of the estimated AUC:

```{webr-r}
#| classes: webr-plot

ggplot(
  data.table(auc = auc_results),
  aes(x = auc)
) +
  geom_histogram(
    bins = 25,
    boundary = 0,
    fill = "grey75",
    color = "grey98"
  ) +
  geom_vline(
    xintercept = mean(auc_results),
    linetype = 2
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "AUC",
    y = "Number of samples"
  )
```

> **Even when the population and prediction model remain exactly the same, the performance we observe varies from sample to sample.**

We can use this **sampling distribution** to estimate the mean and standard error of the AUC estimate:

```{webr-r}
mean(auc_results)
sd(auc_results)
```


## One idea to take with you

We have studied many different statistical methods in this course.

But one idea has been with us from the beginning:

> #### **Samples vary.**

Statistical methods help us understand what that variability means for the scientific questions we care about.
